newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Spain paints rosy picture of economy, EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain paints rosy picture of economy, EMU.

text.p: Spain's central bank governor, Luis Angel Rojo, painted a rosy picture of his country's economic state on Wednesday, predicting it would meet EMU criteria and sustain them for long afterwards.

At a hearing before a European Parliament committee, Rojo said the government's economic policy had borne fruit and that Spain's public deficit as a ratio of Gross Domestic Product was heading way below that required for the single currency.
"Our budget is now sound," he said. "Before the year 2000, we will have a public deficit of 1.5 percent or 1.6 percent of GDP."
The Maastricht Treaty criteria for European Union economic and monetary union (EMU) includes a requirement that deficits this year be no more than 3 percent of GDP and that this be sustainable.
Rojo said everything was on track for Spain to meet the deficit test this year.
"The national bank is convinced we will achieve our objectives this year, the 2.9 or 3.0 percent of GDP," he said.
But meeting EMU targets was not the only reason for budgetary control.

"The Bank of Spain doesn't see our economic policy as only determined by the Maastricht criteria," Rojo said. "We feel our objectives should be long-term.... We have to see that there is reasonable growth. We have to see that jobs are created."
Spain was until relatively recently considered an unlikely member of the first wave of counties to adopt the single EU currency on January 1, 1999.
But a combination of stringent budget and monetary policy turned things around, Rojo said, admitting that it was not altogether expected.
"It was a surprise to all that there were such positive developments," he said.
In addition to the fall in the deficit ratio, Rojo said inflation had declined sharply and become stable. It was not expected to rise above 2 percent on an annual basis either this year or next.
"There has been no increase in inflation (this year). It is following the trend we expected," he told the Euro-MPs.
Economic growth, meanwhile, was solid, hitting 2.9 percent on an annual basis in the first quarter of the year and rising to 3.0 percent on an annual basis in April.
But Rojo said that while he did not expect it, much more growth would not be welcome. "We don't want any extreme growth in the coming months'" he said.

Unemployment remain a major problem, particularly among young people where the jobless rate was over 40 percent, and among women. Stable growth was needed in Spain and across Europe to eat into the problem.
Rojo said Spain's debt to GDP ratio -- above the 60 percent set for EMU -- would not be a problem.
He said the figure was decreasing and was smaller than those in other countries expected to make EMU's first wave. It was also, he said, not a criterion that much bothered financial markets.
